Appendix A. Classification criteria and decision logic To strengthen the classification of strategies within the three resilience capacities—robustness, adaptability, and transformability—the research team conducted an expert consultation process. Initially, experts were briefed on the conceptual distinctions among the three capacities, emphasizing the depth of change each implies for wineries. A subsequent focus group was organized, in which participants discussed the applicability of this methodological framework to the wine sector and reached a consensus on the most appropriate decision model. • Robustness. Strategies were classified as robustness when they did not imply any structural or functional modification within the winery but rather the maintenance or continuity of existing practices (strategies 10–29). For example, the continuation of communication strategies was interpreted as a manifestation of robustness, as it reflects persistence rather than change. • Adaptability. When a strategy involved change but not a qualitative transformation—such as reinforcing, adjusting, or scaling up an already established practice—it was categorized as adaptability. This group includes strategies related to adjustment and reinforcement (strategies 1–4 and 9). • Incremental strategies. Strategies involving an increase in activity or investment were further differentiated. Those implying significant trans- formations—such as expansions in company size or vineyard and winery investments—were classified under transformability (strategies 30–32). Conversely, incremental actions that represented adaptive extensions of existing practices (e.g., managerial improvements or direct sales) were considered adaptability (strategies 5–6). • Transformative changes. Most strategies implying qualitative shifts in the organization or its operations were categorized as transformability (strategies 33, 34, 37, 38). The only exception was the renewal of barrels and tanks (strategy 7), which was deemed part of regular operational maintenance and therefore classified as adaptability. • Investments and innovation. All investment-related strategies were categorized as transformability (strategies 41–43), as were the development of new wines and grape varieties (strategies 36 and 44) and the construction of new facilities (strategy 35). • Technological strategies. The introduction of new technologies was classified depending on their transformative potential. The adoption of digitalization and artificial intelligence tools (strategies 39–40) was deemed transformability, while the incorporation of new software (strategy 8) was interpreted as a routine update and thus assigned to adaptability. Decision logic If no change or modification was identified → robustness (strategies 10–29). JSON: Name: causal_attributes_resilience_wineries Title: Causal estimation of firm attributes' effects on robustness, adaptability, and transformability in rural agro-industries using instrumental variables and propensity-score methods: evidence from Spanish wineries Short Hypothesis: Increasing product and channel diversity causally decreases robustness and causally increases adaptability and transformability among wineries, conditional on firm size, legal form, and perceived external challenges. Related Work: Existing research on resilience in agriculture and wine firms uses two dominant approaches: indicator-based assessments that aggregate ecological and socioeconomic metrics, and perceived-resilience surveys that capture managers' anticipatory judgments. Prior empirical work frequently applies cross-sectional OLS or descriptive methods to relate firm attributes (size, PDO membership, innovation, diversification, rural embeddedness) to resilience proxies. Limitations in current approaches include failure to address endogeneity and reverse causality between attributes and perceived resilience, reliance on single-method measurement (perceptions or structural indicators) without triangulation, inconsistent classification of strategies across robustness/adaptability/transformability domains, limited treatment of sample selection and nonresponse bias, and weak external validity outside studied regions. Few studies implement causal-identification techniques, formal measurement models, or combine objective outcomes with perceived capacities, leaving unresolved whether observed associations reflect causal effects or confounding. Abstract: This research pipeline aims to produce causal estimates of how firm-level attributes (diversification, territorial embeddedness, innovation orientation, size, and legal form) affect three resilience capacities—robustness, adaptability, and transformability—in rural agro-industries, using Spanish wineries as the empirical setting. The approach integrates a validated measurement model for perceived resilience indices with causal-inference methods: propensity-score methods for balancing observed confounders and instrumental-variable estimation to address remaining endogeneity. Data sources combine a manager survey (N=411), firm financials, PDO registry, climatic exposure metrics, and regional demographic indicators. Main contributions are: (1) rigorous causal estimates of attribute effects on each resilience capacity; (2) a measurement-validation step linking subjective and objective resilience indicators; and (3) robustness checks using machine-learning prediction and sensitivity analysis to unobserved confounding. Expected outcomes include quantified trade-offs between diversification and robustness, and policy-relevant identification of attributes most likely to promote adaptive and transformative pathways. Experiments: Datasets: (A) Primary manager survey of Spanish wineries (N=411) containing Likert and binary strategy responses; (B) SABI firm-level financials (turnover, assets, employees); (C) PDO/PGI registry and membership; (D) regional climatic exposure panel (drought/frost indices by municipality); (E) regional demographic indicators (rurality, population change). Baselines: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) with robust standard errors; confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) measurement model; random forest prediction. Causal estimators: propensity-score matching (nearest neighbor and kernel), inverse-probability weighting (IPW), and two-stage least squares (2SLS) with instruments. Instruments: historical PDO presence or historical vineyard density and distance to nearest major export hub; validate instrument relevance and exclusion via first-stage F-statistics and overidentification tests. Outcomes: three continuous indices (robustness, adaptability, transformability) constructed by CFA and standardized; secondary objective outcomes: turnover growth and export share. Covariates: firm age, size (# employees), legal form (cooperative vs private), perceived economic/environmental/social challenges, regional controls. Evaluation metrics: ATE and 2SLS coefficient estimates with 95% CIs, standardized effect sizes, RMSE and R^2 for prediction, variable importance for random forest, balance diagnostics (standardized mean differences), first-stage F-stat, Hansen J test, sensitivity metrics (Rosenbaum bounds and E-values). Experimental setup: (1) validate CFA measurement model and compute indices; (2) run OLS; (3) compute propensity scores and estimate matched and IPW ATEs for key binary attributes (diversification high vs low); (4) run 2SLS for continuous attributes to obtain causal slopes; (5) ablation studies: (a) drop perceived challenge controls, (b) replace perceived indices with objective outcomes, (c) split sample by legal form and size; (6) predictive baseline: train random forest to predict resilience indices using cross-validated hyperparameter tuning (5-fold CV) and compare variable importance; (7) sensitivity analysis to unobserved confounding and weak instruments. All regressions use clustered robust standard errors at regional level and correct for multiple hypothesis testing using false discovery rate. Risk Factors and Limitations: Endogeneity: residual confounding and reverse causality may remain despite PSM and IV; instruments may be weak or violate exclusion. Measurement error: perceived resilience indices derived from Likert items have ordinal scaling and potential reporting bias; triangulation with objective outcomes may be imperfect. Sample bias: 14% survey response rate may induce nonresponse bias and reduce external validity. Statistical power: subgroup analyses (e.g., by legal form) may have limited power. Cross-sectional design: lacks temporal variation to identify dynamic causal effects and long-run adaptation processes. Instrument validity: historical instruments may correlate with unobserved regional factors affecting resilience. Generalization: findings from Spanish wineries may not transfer to other agro-industries or countries with different institutional contexts. Model misspecification: linear IV/OLS assumptions may not hold; heteroskedasticity and nonlinearities could bias estimates. Computation and data linkage: merging multi-source spatial datasets may introduce geocoding error and measurement inconsistency.
